title: Median product "lifespan" has fallen from ~4y down to ~1.5y
selftext:
The "product graveyard" of SaaSHub has been tracking the status (and lifespan) of hundreds of thousands of products. It's been hovering around 4y for quite some time. However, there's a sharp decline in 2026 leading to about 1.5y these days. https://www.saashub.com/product-graveyard That's a huge drop. And, it matches my "human" observations. A lot of products are being vibe coded, released, and soon after that abandoned. It's become too cheap to produce software. So, a lot of people have been experimenting for 'free' with their ideas - only to find out that they weren't viable... or that they couldn't bring customers in. Distribution and marketing have become much more important than before - within the context that everyone can build "features" for free.

Anyhow, I expect this trend of shortening product lifespan to continue even further down. Or maybe, at some point people will realised that there are no users for their products as every user can "build" their own and custom product. Leaving us with a dozen huge platforms that host and help you build those apps. Until then - it's a crazy gold rush and a lot of makers are abandoning their empty buckets.

selftext:

title: "Wrong" Email
selftext:
Let’s say your LinkedIn account has been restricted, and you can no longer access it. You might try to visit:

https://www.linkedin.com//help/linkedin/ask/sdsupport or https://www.linkedin.com//help/linkedin/ask/ppq

to contact customer support. You fill out the form and click "Submit," but for a split second, a pop-up appears:

"we`re sorry. There was an error creating your case. Please try again"

and than redirect.

You might try switching browsers, using private/incognito mode, changing devices (desktop, phone), or even using a different IP address—but nothing works. You keep encountering the same error. However, as soon as you change the email address to one not associated with the restricted account, the form submits successfully. This proves, beyond a doubt, that the "error" was linked solely to the email address; changing the email—while keeping everything else the same—changes the outcome.

Okay, so you’ve submitted the request—what happens next? You receive a response (here are some excerpts; the exact wording may vary slightly):

"You are contacting us from an email address that differs from the one registered to your account."

"An account restriction should not, in itself, prevent you from contacting us via the provided form."

"To protect privacy, I cannot, without a direct request from the account owner sent from their registered email address, do the following:"

"Therefore, please reach out to us using the form mentioned above, ensuring you use the email address registered to your account. This will allow us to proceed with reviewing your inquiry and provide the necessary assistance."

Brilliant. In other words, LinkedIn blocks support requests made using the email address linked to a restricted account—yet when they receive a request made (out of necessity) from a different email address, they close the ticket and instruct you to submit a new one using the "correct" email—which is technically impossible to do. And they are flat-out lying—let me repeat:

An account restriction should not, in itself, prevent you from contacting us via the provided form.

Even if you explicitly point out this situation in your request—and even suggest that they email you directly at the address linked to your account (which they do very, very rarely—maybe once in every 50 attempts)—they still respond with that same template.

This raises two questions:

1. Are the LinkedIn support staff genuinely unaware of this, even though they ought to know? Or do they know, but are lying and moking with users on purpose? I, for one, have never been able to figure this out.

2. Why is so little known about this, given that the situation has persisted for years and has been documented many times ( as example https://youtu.be/RRIm1ReQ_6A?t=221 (t=180) ) ? And why is there no reaction to it? It’s as if it’s been tacitly accepted.

title: Ask HN: Kimi Code hit its 5-hour limit after $1.37 of API usage
selftext:
I paid $19 for Kimi Code to test K3.1 Pro Standard (not Highspeed) using the official CLI v2.3.1.

I ran two tasks on small repositories:

1. Recommend movies based on an existing movie database.
2. Analyze a website's codebase.

Neither task completed. The entire 5-hour quota was exhausted within minutes.

I analyzed the actual session logs, including background agents:

- Fresh input: 368,203 tokens
- Cached input: 1,183,744 tokens
- Output: 39,324 tokens
- Total: 1.59M tokens

At Kimi's published API rates, that's just $1.37 worth of usage before hitting the 5-hour limit which is easily less than 5% of what Claude Code offers at $20 subscription.

The logs show: "429 You've reached your 5-hour usage limit."

For comparison, Claude Code on a $20 subscription processed roughly 381M tokens over 4-5 hours using Opus 5.5 xhigh, mostly cached input. That's not a controlled benchmark, but the difference in usable capacity is staggering.

Both Kimi tasks failed without delivering results. I have video evidence and detailed logs, but won't publish private repository data.

Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hSr-DLn88AM

Is this a quota-accounting bug, or are Kimi's $19 subscription limits intentionally this restrictive?

Disclosure: I also develop a competing coding agent. These tests used Kimi's official CLI.

title: Looking for a tech job is a helpless data-entry nightmare
selftext:
I spent hundred of hours (distributed over many days) filling my resume data to freshly developed forms made specifically to the hiring process of one or two companies, even though I feel like I have a top 10% resume and years of in hands-down software development experience. I love solving problems, it's part of me.

I know it has got a lot harder to land a development gig but I've worked with modern stuff like AI-generated briefs for meetings, bug logs automatically sent emails to responsible developers, at a point I had an Agent dedicated to verifying how well our code was written so I feel like I've kept up with the innovations, and skills.

But I have no idea how to land a job in software development anymore: nothing seems enough. I have tried for over a year and the only reason I can withstand this much waiting while seeking a job in that field is because of my exceptional employment history (including working to Silicon Valley companies), but it has got to a point I am worried.

I've asked my friends who are also developers and they feel similarly, we do not know where to dedicate our effors, as if the competency of software engineers were transformed irrelevant because of AI. We know what happened, we just don't know what to do with all the competency we embody.

I've taken a liking to working as a bartender in my local city, because that's kind of the only job I can land lately, but as soon as my degree in Computer Engineering is mentioned I'm set aside as a anti-social computer expert who will never take a low-paying job like "this". (Secretly I found it very fun, fullfilling in a way I never thought I needed because money was my priority at the beggining of the carreer)

How the hell do we transform this competency and learning ability of software engineers into desireable company-adding value skills?

(I swear this is not generated by AI, I don't even know how to prove anymore)

title: Ask HN: What happened to our collective ethos?
selftext:
I’m an outsider to both Silicon Valley and enterprise IT; I’m just a freelance consultant and web host plying my trade in the suburbs of Charlotte. But I have generally presumed that we all share a common nostalgic ideal rooted in the memories and stories of Bell Labs, Xerox PARC, and their unbound, open-ended exploration of science, technology, and the limits of their imaginations. I’ve been told that the economic and regulatory conditions that allowed these monuments to human endeavor ultimately shifted, monopolies were broken up, assets were sold off, and it ultimately served as the incubator for the modern technology industry.

But we’ve since seen companies emerge with market dominance and wealth that the Bell Group could only dream about, who presided over a decade and a half of near-zero interest rates. None of whom elected to establish/fund public-facing research campuses stuffed with Nobel laureates conducting their own frontier research departments. What’s worse, most of them instead chose to turn their oligopolies towards seeking to control the media and political process, privatizing what was left of America’s public aerospace programs, gatekeeping research and development, and subsidizing their further encroachments with the resulting government contracts.

How are these the people we granted so much power and influence to? Was it simply that Silicon Valley was captured by the financial industry? Was the origin story always a convenient myth, that nobody ever actually took seriously, or objected to when it was cynically exploited by the patently disingenuous and greedy CEOs who have, without exception, acted in the worst interests of their users, society, and the planet? Just the base selfishness of human nature?

Were the research and development labs of the post-war American era just a flash in the pan, or could Silicon Valley someday rediscover its lost soul? I’d reckon we’d all be better off for it, but I am also concerned that I simply fell the for the marketing hype, and there never was the altruistic spirit of innovation I’d always imagined.

title: Ask HN: Can we do something about this impending AI dystopia
selftext:
There have been, increasingly, a large number of posts [1] on HN in the past few weeks, where developers are slowly coming to terms with the breakneck speed with which Agentic Coding has advanced in the past few months.

We all agree that an average software developer today is closely resembling the horse-carriage just when automobiles were becoming mainstream around 120 years ago.

And coming to HN daily and finding at least one such lament from a software engineer is becoming quite tiresome.

We are all, mostly, rational thinkers and worship logic and reasoning even more than our respective gods.

With the context built-up enough, I would like to challenge the community to come up with ways to counter this death march that we find ourselves on. We are now, with every passing day, becoming more and more dependent on Agentic Coding. This is bringing the inevitable end to our profession closer at an exponential rate.

It seems we are like a drug-addict that knows that soon, one day, the drug would be a likely end of him, yet carries on consuming it.

How can we control this?

How do we slow down the pace?

How do we bring it to a halt?

title: Ask HN: Are people aware OpenAI Dots intercept SSL?
selftext:
I've already cancelled my OpenAI subscription due to all their recent shenanigans. But before my month ends I thought I'd see what this Dot thing is all about.

First thing I did was install Firefox to test out a project of mine (wouldn't work in Chrome). It failed to connect:

> The cloud proxy uses an OpenAI certificate authority that the operating system already trusts, but the fresh Firefox profile doesn’t. The game’s connection verifies successfully against that existing authority.

> May I add that same cloud certificate authority to this isolated Firefox test profile? Certificate validation stays enabled, but Firefox would then trust certificates issued by the cloud proxy.

Wait. What? No. Of course not.

Aren't Dots ostensibly designed for personal use? Accessing your email and the like. With this thing intercepting web traffic, I imagine almost everyone using these things are in violation of all sorts of policies and agreements.
author: Benjamin_Dobell

title: PSA: Do not use term "vibe coding"
selftext:
... because it is hopelessly vague and useless.

What does it mean? "Forget that the code even exists AND fully give in to the vibes"? What vibes? How are vibes defined? Are one supposed to dance freestyle on a flat plain? This ain't agentic engineering, that's for sure.

It seems the original coinage was connected to a thought of an AI-led WYSIWYG environment; perhaps connected to a new type of library repository, and managed under a novel source code control system that may or may not be a hard fork of Git. This is much closer to agentic management and graph engineering, but that was not the road the other term took later.

And it certainly doesn't matter now. The best models now are good at doing everything from scratch, uncannily and frighteningly good. So good that there is now a risk of corporate AI budgets no longer growing simply because there won't be anything left to automate in a year or two, tanking the valuation of many decacorn startups and setting up very precarious times ahead.

---

Just my thoughts.

I needed to publish myself.
